_note: Stock ship templates on the ATOMIC model (ADR 0014). Every class is a NUCLEUS of bodies fused directly together - one per proton, capped at eight for practicality - plus a set of EXTREMITIES, one per valence electron, each on its own tunnel with a hatch. Period-1 classes have no extremities at all: a closed first shell has nothing outside it. The whole ship is built to ShipConfig.template_volume_m3 however many bodies that is, so every class encloses the same volume and the classes differ in SHAPE rather than in size - hydrogen spends it all on one module, argon splits it sixteen ways. The extremity geometry comes from the PERIOD (more shells, richer arrangement) and steps up to a larger arrangement when a class has more extremities than the period's own geometry has berths. Nothing here fixes a SIZE or a SHAPE: the volume comes from tuning.json and the room and hallway families are chosen when the template is built. ShipTemplates.build() reads this pack; adding a template must never require touching core/.

single.description: One branch, straight up the spine. The smallest thing that is still two rooms and a tunnel between them.

linear.description: Two branches on one axis, 180 degrees apart - a spine module with a room at each end. VSEPR's linear geometry, and the plan of every corridor ship ever drawn.

bent.description: Two branches at 104.5 degrees, water's own bond angle. Reads as a hab module with two wings that do not quite face each other, which is exactly why it is the shape everybody recognises.

trigonal.description: Three branches at 120 degrees in one plane. The flattest arrangement that still surrounds the core, and the cheapest to dock at because every tunnel mouth is reachable from the same approach.

pyramidal.description: Three branches swept below the equator, ammonia's trigonal pyramid. The lopsided one: the core keeps a clear face on top, which is where a bridge or a dorsal mast goes.

tetrahedral.description: Four branches at 109.5 degrees, the carbon plan. The most symmetric way to put four rooms around one without any two tunnels sharing a plane, and the reason a methane-pattern hull looks equally sane from every angle.

square.description: Four branches at 90 degrees in one plane - the same four rooms as tetrahedral, laid flat. Squarer, more industrial, and it stacks: two square modules on a shared spine make a deck.

bipyramidal.description: Five branches: three around the waist and one at each pole. Phosphorus geometry, and the first arrangement with two genuinely different kinds of berth - equatorial and axial - which is where a ship starts having a bow.

octahedral.description: Six branches on the three axes, sulphur's plan. A room in every direction: no bow, no stern, no up. Cramped, symmetrical and completely disorienting inside, which some crews are said to prefer.

pentagonal.description: Seven branches: five around the waist plus both poles. Past this the tunnel mouths start crowding each other on the core's surface, which is a real structural limit and not a rendering one.

cubic.description: Eight branches on the corners of a cube - the full shell, every diagonal occupied. The densest arrangement the eight-children-per-part limit allows, and it looks it.

1.description: One shell and nothing outside it. Period-1 classes have no extremities at all, so this is the geometry they never use.

2.description: Two shells: the extremities spread in one plane. The flattest arrangement that still surrounds the core, and the cheapest to bring a hull alongside.

3.description: Three shells: the extremities leave the plane. No two tunnels share a face, which is what stops a third-row hull reading as a stack of discs.

4.description: Four shells: the extremities square up. Flat again, but at four berths rather than three, and it stacks with its own kind.

5.description: Five shells: a waist and two poles, the first geometry with two genuinely different kinds of berth on one hull.

6.description: Six shells: a berth on every axis. No bow, no stern, no up.

7.description: Seven shells: the corners of a cube, every diagonal occupied. The densest the eight-children rule allows.

hydrogen.label: Hydrogen
hydrogen.description: One module, and the whole volume budget spent on it. The largest single room any class gets: no nucleus to share with, no extremities to feed, just a hull you can cross without passing a hatch. Every other class is this ship cut up and rearranged.

helium.label: Helium
helium.description: Two nucleus bodies fused into one mass, half the budget each. A closed shell needs nothing outside it, so there are no extremities and no tunnels at all - the shortest possible ship that is still two rooms, and the only one where both of them are core.

lithium.label: Lithium
lithium.description: A three-body nucleus with a single arm off it. The first class with an outside: one extremity, one tunnel, one hatch, and a core that is already big enough to have a middle. Light, lopsided and cheap to dock.

beryllium.label: Beryllium
beryllium.description: Four fused into the core and two arms reaching off it. The first class with a THROUGH line - a crew can cross it end to end without turning around - which is why yards keep reaching for it when the customer wants a shuttle rather than a station.

boron.label: Boron
boron.description: Five in the nucleus, three extremities spread around it. The first class that surrounds its own core: no matter where you approach from, an arm is pointing somewhere near you. Awkward to berth, hard to lose.

carbon.label: Carbon
carbon.description: Six fused into the core, four arms off it, no two tunnels sharing a plane. The workhorse: it takes load evenly from every direction, it reads as deliberate from any angle, and it is what every yard builds when nobody has said what the ship is for.

nitrogen.label: Nitrogen
nitrogen.description: A seven-body nucleus carrying five arms. The core is now most of the ship by mass and the extremities are genuinely small - the first class that reads as a station with tenders docked rather than as a vessel with wings.

oxygen.label: Oxygen
oxygen.description: The nucleus at its full eight, six arms around it on the three axes. There is no bow and no stern left: every direction has a room in it, and the core is a solid block of hull with the whole crew arranged on its surface.

fluorine.label: Fluorine
fluorine.description: Eight fused, seven arms - one shy of a full shell, and the gap is the point. Every fluorine hull has exactly one clear face, which is where the yards put the dock, the drive, or whatever the customer would rather not run a corridor past.

neon.label: Neon
neon.description: Eight in the core and eight arms on the corners of a cube. The full shell: the densest arrangement the eight-children rule allows, sixteen rooms of five hundred cubic metres each, and not one face of the core left unused.

sodium.label: Sodium
sodium.description: A full eight-body nucleus and a single long arm. The third-row classes push their extremities further out, so this reads as a heavy core towing one distant pod - a tug, a tender, or a station with one thing it needs to keep at arm's length.

silicon.label: Silicon
silicon.description: Carbon's four arms on a third-row frame: the same berth count, the same tetrahedral spread, a heavier core and longer tunnels. Where carbon is compact, this is roomy - the difference a yard sells as 'the same plan, but you can get a loader down the corridor'.

phosphorus.label: Phosphorus
phosphorus.description: Five arms off a full nucleus: three around the waist and one at each pole. The first class with two genuinely different KINDS of berth, which is why it turns up wherever a ship needs to treat its poles differently from its flanks.

sulphur.label: Sulphur
sulphur.description: Six arms on the three axes off a heavy third-row core. Symmetrical, cramped and complete - the same plan as oxygen with more room between the extremities, which is the whole reason anyone picks it over oxygen.

chlorine.label: Chlorine
chlorine.description: Seven arms and one clear face, on a third-row frame. Fluorine's plan with the reach to use it: the gap is big enough to bring something large alongside without threading it between two tunnels.

argon.label: Argon
argon.description: The full shell at third-row spacing: eight fused in the core, eight arms on the cube's corners, sixteen bodies of five hundred cubic metres. The largest part count any class reaches, and the plainest statement of what the volume budget buys.

water.label: Water Molecule
water.description: An oxygen-pattern core with a hydrogen module on each of its two bent berths - the ship everybody draws when they are asked to draw a small ship. Two hab pods at 104.5 degrees off a central utility core, one tunnel each, one hatch at every end. Cramped, obvious, and completely serviceable.

methane.label: Methane Module
methane.description: A carbon core with all four tetrahedral berths filled. The stock four-pod hull: no two pods share a plane, so it takes thrust from any direction without twisting, and every pod is the same distance from the galley. The yards sell more of these than everything else combined.

ammonia.label: Ammonia Tender
ammonia.description: A nitrogen core with three pods swept below it and the dorsal face left bare for a mast. The classic working tender: everything crew-related hangs underneath where it is easy to reach from a dock, and everything that has to see out goes on top.

carbon_dioxide.label: Carbon Dioxide Spine
carbon_dioxide.description: A carbon core with an oxygen module on each end of one axis - a long, straight, three-module spine. The cheapest way to make a ship that is genuinely bigger than one room, and the plan of most short-haul freight in service.

ethane.label: Ethane Barge
ethane.description: Two carbon cores joined by a single tunnel, each carrying three pods. The first pattern in the catalogue with two junctions instead of one, which means it has a middle - and a middle is where a barge puts its cargo.

hydrogen_peroxide.label: Peroxide Chain
hydrogen_peroxide.description: Two oxygen cores joined end to end with a pod on the far side of each - a four-module chain with a kink in the middle. Long, thin and slightly twisted, which is what happens when you build a ship out of two bent cores instead of one straight one.
